clue.text: Could it be twelve inches wide ?

definitions.text: Could it be twelve inches wide ?

parts.words: Could it be twelve inches wide ?
parts.note: twelve inches make one imperial foot, so the clue pictures a walkway exactly that measure across

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a thing really measures a foot across.
explanation.walkthrough: Twelve inches is a foot, so a walkers' track can be read as a path one foot wide.
explanation.definitionFit: A pedestrian walkway beside a road or across fields is the everyday meaning; the clue reads it literally as a track of one foot's width.

clue.text: Utopian variety of prickly pear

indicators.note: a variety is a different version, so the letters of the next word appear in a new order

explanation.surface: An idealistic cultivar of a cactus fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety of' rearranges UTOPIAN; the answer is the botanical genus of the prickly pear cactus.
explanation.definitionFit: The genus name of the cactus that bears the prickly pear fruit, sometimes used for the plant itself.

clue.text: But not the weapons of World War I

definitions.text: But not the weapons of World War I

parts.words: But not the weapons of World War I
parts.note: British soldiers of the Great War were nicknamed Tommies, but the submachine guns named for Thompson came later

explanation.surface: A remark that certain guns were not those of the 1914-18 war.
explanation.walkthrough: British soldiers were 'Tommies', so their guns might seem to fit; but the Thompson submachine gun was not used in World War I.
explanation.definitionFit: The Thompson submachine gun was a 1920s American weapon, not the rifles carried by British Tommies of the trenches.

clue.text: A sailor has a way with him, but not at home

parts.note: AB, able-bodied seaman, is a sailor
a road is a way

explanation.surface: A seaman takes a path with him but is away from his house.
explanation.walkthrough: AB (able seaman) is a common crossword sailor; 'has ... with him' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Overseas or out of one's own country, not in the home country.

clue.text: Striking result of having low aims

definitions.text: Striking result of having low aims

parts.words: Striking result of having low aims
parts.note: in boxing, aiming a punch too low gives a foul blow; low aims also suggests base ambitions

explanation.surface: A comment on what comes of being unambitious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'low aims' reads as poor ambition, but a boxer aiming low strikes below the waistband, a foul, which also means an unfair attack.
explanation.definitionFit: A foul punch below the waistband in boxing, and figuratively any unfair attack.

clue.text: Models are re-shaped, but not often

indicators.note: something re-shaped has been given a new form, so the letters of the word before are rearranged

explanation.surface: Fashion models are made over, but only now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: 're-shaped' tells you to rearrange the six letters of MODELS.
explanation.definitionFit: Rarely, only on infrequent occasions, is a straight synonym.

clue.text: Careless example of hit and run

parts.note: slap means to hit
dash means to run

explanation.surface: A hit-and-run driving incident shows recklessness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit and run' suggests a driving offence; here hit and run are two separate pieces placed side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: Hasty and sloppy, done without proper attention.

clue.text: Hugh is their. 'operatic representative

parts.note: Vaughan Williams wrote the opera Hugh the Drover, whose hero represents the cattle-drivers' trade

explanation.surface: A man called Hugh speaks for some group in the opera.
explanation.walkthrough: Hugh the Drover is a 1924 opera by Ralph Vaughan Williams; its hero stands for all who herd livestock to market.
explanation.definitionFit: Men who herd cattle or sheep to market, whose trade is shown on stage by Vaughan Williams's hero.

clue.text: They postpone the day of reckoning

definitions.text: They postpone the day of reckoning

parts.words: They postpone the day of reckoning
parts.note: legal suspensions of payment or activity put off the time when debts must be settled

explanation.surface: Things that delay judgement day.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural form of the word for an authorised suspension, here of debt payment.
explanation.definitionFit: Authorised delays or suspensions, especially of debt repayment, which defer settlement.

clue.text: French walls are sound

parts.note: mur is the French word for a wall, and two walls give it twice
the second wall, again the French word mur

explanation.surface: Walls in France are said to be in good repair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective meaning solid, but it is the noun: a low continuous noise. The plural 'walls' asks for the French word twice.
explanation.definitionFit: A low, indistinct continuous noise, like voices heard through a partition, is a kind of sound.

clue.text: Stage fitting for a drop scene

definitions.text: Stage fitting for a drop scene

parts.words: Stage fitting for a drop scene
parts.note: a theatre fixture in the floor through which an actor can fall out of sight, punning on the drop scene, a painted curtain

explanation.surface: A piece of theatre equipment used when the painted backcloth comes down.
explanation.walkthrough: A drop scene is a painted curtain lowered on stage; here the 'drop' is a performer falling through a hatch in the boards.
explanation.definitionFit: A hinged hatch in a theatre floor lets a performer vanish below, so it is a stage fixture for dropping.

clue.text: A woman was once bound to' get tight with this

definitions.text: A woman was once bound to' get tight with this

parts.words: A woman was once bound to' get tight with this
parts.note: old-fashioned corsets were drawn tight with a cord, so the woman was bound by it, not obliged to get drunk

explanation.surface: A woman of earlier times was sure to end up drunk thanks to this.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bound to get tight' reads as 'certain to become drunk', but means literally tied up and pulled tight in a corset.
explanation.definitionFit: A cord threaded through a corset was pulled to cinch the waist of a Victorian lady.

clue.text: Address in a straightforward manner

explanation.surface: Speak to someone plainly.
explanation.definitionFit: To aim words or a letter at someone is one sense; frank and without detour is the other, used adverbially as in 'go straight there'.

clue.text: Shakespearian doctor at College

explanation.surface: A physician from Shakespeare working at a university college.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Caius is the French physician in The Merry Wives of Windsor; Gonville and Caius is a Cambridge college, often called by the second name alone.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense names the French physician in Shakespeare's Merry Wives of Windsor; the other is the short name of a Cambridge college.

clue.text: Patently obvious instruction to transcribers

parts.note: an order to copy correctly, and 'patently' hints at legal protection of written work

explanation.surface: Clearly self-evident advice for copyists.
explanation.walkthrough: Split it in two and it tells a copyist to copy correctly; whole, it is the legal right protecting authors, as patents protect inventors.
explanation.definitionFit: The legal protection of an author's work, like a patent for inventions; read in two parts, it tells copyists to get it correct.

clue.text: He undoubtedly has something

parts.note: read as a compliment about a talented person, but literally it describes an owner, who by definition has a thing

explanation.surface: A remark that some man certainly has talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has something' sounds like praise for a gifted person; read literally it describes whoever owns a thing.
explanation.definitionFit: An owner or holder is one who keeps property, so he certainly has something.

clue.text: Did these cyclists leave a cinder track ?

definitions.text: Did these cyclists leave a cinder track ?

parts.words: Did these cyclists leave a cinder track ?
parts.note: speeding cyclists were called ..., as if they burned the road behind them; a cinder track is also a racing surface

explanation.surface: A question whether some cyclists raced on a cinder-surfaced circuit.
explanation.walkthrough: Early slang for reckless fast cyclists suggests they burned the road, leaving cinders behind.
explanation.definitionFit: Late-Victorian slang for cyclists who rode furiously fast, as if burning up the road.

clue.text: Fellow-actor ?

parts.note: a companion in games read as a mate in a stage play

explanation.surface: Someone on the same stage.
explanation.walkthrough: A child's companion in games, reread as a mate in a stage play.
explanation.definitionFit: A companion one plays with, read here as a colleague in a drama.

clue.text: Convert to _ poetry, Les, though, starting otherwise

indicators.note: the letters set off in a different order, so the words before are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone urges Les to switch to writing verse, though he started out differently.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting otherwise' tells you to rearrange POETRY and LES; 'Convert' looks like a verb but is the noun, a person won over to a faith.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who has changed religion or opinion is a new recruit to the cause, as in a zealous newcomer to a church.

clue.text: Do hikers" garments last longer ?

parts.note: a verb meaning to last longer than, also read as clothes for outdoors

explanation.surface: A question about the durability of walking clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb means to outlast; split, it suggests outdoor clothing such as hikers wear.
explanation.definitionFit: To last longer than something else; read as two words it is clothing for outdoors.

clue.text: The composer was so attached to his country

parts.note: the composer was American, so his country is the USA

explanation.surface: A composer is said to have been very fond of his homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: John Philip Sousa, the American march composer; 'attached to' just joins the two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: John Philip Sousa was an American composer of marches such as The Stars and Stripes Forever.

clue.text: With which Egyptians 'became rattled ?

parts.note: the ancient Egyptian temple instrument was shaken to make a rattling sound, not to unnerve anyone

explanation.surface: A question about what upset the people of Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'became rattled' suggests losing composure; literally the Egyptians rattled the metal instrument in worship.
explanation.definitionFit: A metal-framed rattle used in ancient Egyptian worship, especially of Isis.

clue.text: He might get drunk at the gate

definitions.text: He might get drunk at the gate

parts.words: He might get drunk at the gate
parts.note: a gatekeeper shares his name with a dark beer, which would be drunk

explanation.surface: A man who could end up intoxicated at the entrance.
explanation.walkthrough: A gatekeeper shares his name with a dark beer, so 'he' could be drunk in the sense of swallowed.
explanation.definitionFit: A doorkeeper at a gate, and also a dark brown beer that is drunk.

clue.text: Club for' roundsmen'?

parts.note: a society whose members take turns in rotation, punning on roundsmen, tradesmen doing delivery rounds

explanation.surface: A social club for milkmen and other delivery men.
explanation.walkthrough: A roundsman delivers on a round; the club meant is the international service club whose name comes from members hosting in rotation.
explanation.definitionFit: The service club for business people takes its name from members once hosting meetings in turn, going round.

clue.text: His employers are liable to become dispirited

definitions.text: His employers are liable to become dispirited

parts.words: His employers are liable to become dispirited
parts.note: those who hire him are rid of spirits, a demon cast out, not made sad

explanation.surface: Anyone who hires this man tends to lose heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dispirited' normally means downcast; here it means freed of evil spirits, which is what the cleric is hired to do.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleric who casts out demons leaves the possessed person free of spirits.

clue.text: It wasn't really a fair burden she carried

definitions.text: It wasn't really a fair burden she carried

parts.words: It wasn't really a fair burden she carried
parts.note: from the proverb that the wife who rules her husband is the better horse; 'fair' puns on blonde, the animal not being fair-coated

explanation.surface: A remark that some woman shouldered an unjust load.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'the grey mare is the better horse' means the wife rules the household. A grey horse is not fair in colour, and a mare carries a burden.
explanation.definitionFit: A pale, ash-coloured female horse is a beast of burden, not a fair or blonde one; the phrase also names a dominant wife.

clue.text: He is in the right party for speculation

indicators.note: the first word sits inside the second, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: the Tories are the right-wing party in British politics

explanation.surface: A man belongs to the right-wing party, for what it is worth.
explanation.walkthrough: The Conservatives are Britain's party of the right; 'He' looks like the subject of the sentence but is just two letters to be placed.
explanation.definitionFit: A hypothesis or conjecture not yet proved is a speculation.

clue.text: High chair ? None more so

parts.note: not a child's seat but a monarch's seat of state, the loftiest seat of all

explanation.surface: A remark about a baby's tall feeding seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High chair' suggests a baby's feeding seat; the real sense is a seat of the highest rank.
explanation.definitionFit: A sovereign's ceremonial seat is the most exalted chair there is.

clue.text: It's tedious with an, unspecified number to dress

parts.note: tire is an old verb meaning to dress or attire
some means an indefinite quantity

explanation.surface: Getting a crowd of people dressed is a bore.
explanation.walkthrough: TIRE is an archaic word for dress, as in attire.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearisome, dull and boring are synonyms.
